overview.title: 📖 Overview: Causing and Penalizing a Blemish
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 34a–34b
overview.hebrewSource: הַצּוֹרֵם אוֹזֶן בַּבְּכוֹר — הֲרֵי זֶה לֹא יִשְׁחוֹט עוֹלָמִית, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר. וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: נוֹלַד בּוֹ מוּם אַחֵר — יִשְׁחוֹט עָלָיו
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara first closes out the previous discussion, extending the ban on blemishing a firstborn to indirect methods, and using the same tannaitic dispute to explain a parallel disagreement about safeguarding doubtfully-impure teruma. A new mishna then asks: if someone deliberately slits a firstborn's ear to disqualify it, may the animal ever be slaughtered? Rabbi Eliezer says never — even if a genuine blemish later appears naturally — while the Rabbis allow slaughter once an unrelated blemish develops. The Gemara compares this penalty to a similar one in the laws of leprosy, works out a subtle textual question about a bridegroom, and finally asks whether the penalty on a firstborn passes down to the transgressor's son after his death.

slides.title: 🐕 Even an Indirect Blemish Is Forbidden
slides.hebrewSource: מִנַּיִן שֶׁלֹּא יָבִיא דְּבֵילָה וּבָצֵק וְיַנִּיחֶנָּה עַל הָאוֹזֶן כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּבֹא כֶּלֶב וְיֹאכְלֶנָּה? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״כׇּל מוּם״
slides.label: The question:
slides.text: From where do we know one may not place pressed figs or dough on a firstborn's ear so that a dog comes and bites it off, causing a blemish without the owner's own hand doing the deed? The verse's phrase 'there shall not be any blemish in it' (Leviticus 22:21) is read to include a blemish caused indirectly, not only one caused directly.

slides.title: 📜 'My Terumot' — One Word, Two Readings
slides.subtitle: The same textual method resolves the earlier dispute about the barrel of doubtful teruma

lines.speaker: Verse
lines.text: Numbers 18:8: 'And I, behold, I have given you the charge of מִשְׁמֶרֶת תְּרוּמֹתָי — My terumot' — written in the plural.

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: Two terumot are meant: one definitely pure, one in doubt (teruma teluya). Both must be safeguarded from impurity.

lines.speaker: R' Yehoshua
lines.text: Read it as terumati, 'My teruma' — singular. Only teruma fit for you, i.e. definitely pure, need be guarded.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Does Rabbi Eliezer really rely on pronunciation over spelling? A baraita on בְּבִגְדוֹ בָּהּ shows the opposite: there, Rabbi Akiva reads by pronunciation, Rabbi Eliezer by spelling!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Not a contradiction — the real dispute here is different: R' Yehoshua says safeguard only what is 'fit for you' (definitely pure); R' Eliezer says doubtful teruma is also 'fit', since Elijah may yet come and declare it pure.

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: The dispute is resolved not by a rule about vocalization, but by what counts as teruma 'fit for you' to safeguard.

slides.title: ✂️ New Mishna: Slitting a Firstborn's Ear
slides.subtitle: How permanent is the penalty for deliberately causing a blemish?

nodes.content: ❓ One deliberately slits (צורם) a firstborn's ear to disqualify it. May it ever be slaughtered?

columns.label: Rabbi Eliezer
columns.content: Never — the animal may never be slaughtered, even if a genuine new blemish later develops naturally

columns.label: The Rabbis
columns.content: Once another, unrelated blemish develops on its own, the animal may be slaughtered on account of that one

nodes.content: 🤔 Objection: does Rabbi Eliezer really impose penalties forever? In the laws of leprosy (נגעים) he limits the penalty for one who excised a leprous mark to heal only once a new mark appears

✅ Rabba and Rav Yosef: a penalty on property (the firstborn) must be indefinite, or people would blemish freely; a penalty on the body (leprosy) needs no such severity, since no one wants to be sick again

callout.label: Rava's follow-up:
callout.text: The Rabbis' own two rulings also seemed to conflict (limited for bechor, stricter for leprosy) — resolved the same way: in each case the Sages penalize precisely the means the transgressor used to try to profit.

slides.title: 👰 One Letter, One Practical Difference
slides.hebrewSource: לִכְשֶׁיִּוָּלֵד לוֹ נֶגַע אַחֵר יִטְהַר הֵימֶנּוּ / וְיִטְהָר
slides.label: Rav Pappa's dilemma:
slides.text: Did Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on the excised leprous mark say yit'har (he becomes pure immediately once the new mark appears) or veyit'har (he stays impure from the old mark until the new mark is itself confirmed pure)? The practical difference: a bridegroom is granted seven days of wedding celebrations before any new mark is examined. If 'yit'har' is correct, he is fully pure the whole week; if 'veyit'har,' he remains impure from the old mark throughout — even though the new mark isn't checked yet. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved: תֵּיקוּ.

slides.title: 👨‍👦 Does the Penalty Reach the Son?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: if the father dies, is the son bound too?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Case 1 for comparison: one who sells his Canaanite slave to gentiles and dies — the son IS penalized (must redeem the slave), since every day the slave is denied mitzvot
2️⃣ Case 2 for comparison: one who intends prohibited labor on Chol HaMoed but dies before doing it — the son is NOT penalized, since no prohibited act was ever performed
3️⃣ Neither case matches cleanly: does the penalty attach to the man himself (who is now gone) or to his property (the animal, still owned by his heirs)?

4️⃣ Resolution from Shevi'it: a field improved (fertilized) unlawfully during the Sabbatical Year may not be sown afterward — but if the improver dies, his son may sow it. The penalty binds only the transgressor, not his heir

callout.label: Conclusion:
callout.text: By analogy, the son of one who slit the firstborn's ear is not bound by his late father's penalty.

summary.principle: The Torah's ban on blemishing a firstborn covers indirect methods too, and the Sages impose penalties calibrated to deter — permanent when property is at stake, limited when the body is, and never inherited by an innocent heir.

flowSteps.content: 🐕 'Any blemish' includes one caused indirectly, e.g. luring a dog to bite the ear
📜 'My terumot' (plural/singular) settles whether doubtfully-impure teruma must be safeguarded

columns.content: ✂️ R' Eliezer: slitting the ear bars slaughter forever
✂️ Rabbis: a later, natural blemish permits slaughter

flowSteps.content: 👨‍👦 The penalty attaches to the transgressor's property, not to his son as heir
🎓 Key Principle: penalties track intent and means — property penalties must be severe enough to deter, but they end with the transgressor himself

quiz.q: Why is placing dough on a firstborn's ear so a dog bites it off also forbidden, according to the Gemara?
o: It is not forbidden, since the owner did not act directly
The verse 'there shall not be any blemish in it' includes blemishes caused indirectly, not just directly
Dogs are inherently forbidden near consecrated animals
Only priests may cause blemishes
quiz.e: The word 'any' (כׇּל) in 'there shall not be any blemish in it' is read to include indirect causation of a blemish, not only a direct act.

quiz.q: What is the basis of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua over safeguarding a barrel of doubtful teruma?
o: Whether teruma may ever be eaten by non-priests
Whether 'My terumot' (Numbers 18:8) refers to two types of teruma, including doubtful teruma, or only to teruma that is definitely pure and thus 'fit for you'
Whether the barrel belongs to the priest or the farmer
Whether teruma requires a blessing before eating
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer reads the plural as including doubtful teruma (since Elijah may yet purify it); Rabbi Yehoshua limits the safeguarding requirement to teruma definitely fit to eat.

quiz.q: In the new mishna, what does Rabbi Eliezer rule about a firstborn whose ear was deliberately slit?
o: It may be slaughtered immediately
It may never be slaughtered, even if another blemish later develops naturally
It must be given to a gentile
It becomes permanently non-sacred
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer imposes a permanent penalty: the animal may never be slaughtered on account of any blemish, even one that develops naturally afterward.

quiz.q: How do Rabba and Rav Yosef explain why Rabbi Eliezer's penalty for blemishing a firstborn is permanent, while his penalty for excising a leprous mark is limited?
o: There is no real difference between the two rulings
A penalty on property (like a firstborn) must be severe to prevent abuse, while a penalty on the body (like leprosy) does not need to be, since no one wants to remain sick
Leprosy is a more severe sin than blemishing an offering
Rabbi Eliezer changed his opinion over time
quiz.e: Since a person suffers no personal harm from blemishing his firstborn (only benefiting financially), the deterrent must be permanent; but no one seeks to remain leprous, so a lesser deterrent suffices there.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma about whether the ear-slitting penalty passes to the transgressor's son after his death?
o: It remains permanently unresolved (teiku)
By analogy to a Sabbatical Year law: one who unlawfully improves (fertilizes) a field and dies — his son may still sow it — showing the penalty binds only the transgressor, not his heir
By ruling that the son is always penalized like his father
By comparing it only to the Canaanite slave case, concluding the son is penalized
quiz.e: The Sheviit case demonstrates that such penalties are personal to the transgressor: the son of one who unlawfully improved his field may sow it, so the son of one who slit the ear likely is not bound by the penalty either.
